Sample.evidence_source: [/page/3/Text/3] This article, part of a wider study of prison leavers' mental health needs (Howerton et al. 2007), addresses two specific research questions with a view to informing suicide prevention strategies, namely: how do offenders explain their own and others' suicide attempts? And what leads some offenders, but not others, to attempt suicide?

Population.evidence_source: [/page/3/Text/3] We could identify no qualitative studies specifically examining suicide attempts by offenders outside of prison. This article, part of a wider study of prison leavers' mental health needs (Howerton et al. 2007), addresses two specific research questions with a view to informing suicide prevention strategies, namely: how do offenders explain their own and others' suicide attempts? Population.warning: The review is for male suicide, and 'offenders' is not gender-specified, so inferring male.

Area.evidence_source: [/page/2/Text/5] This more restricted agency is perhaps associated with hopelessness and fractured reflexivity, and also to suicide attempts. On the other hand, high levels of agency may be needed to succeed in taking one's own life. This tension is evident clinically as, when assessing suicide risk, both hopelessness and a clear intent to suicidal behaviour are the considered key markers of risk for current and future attempts (Harriss et al. 2005, Morris et al. 2013) and intent, as interpreted by clinicians, can be seen as a form of agency.
